La réinsertion sociale et le milieu carc: Social Reintegration and the Prison System: The Great Forgotten Issues of Public Debate
« Je ne crois plus à la réinsertion, ça: “I don’t believe in reintegration anymore, it never worked for me”
Trois hommes aux identités racialisées,: Three racialized men who have been incarcerated reflect on the challenges of social reintegration Illustration: Nia E-K
Au Canada et au Québec, les minorités vi: In Canada and in Quebec, visible minorities are overrepresented in correctional facilities: in recent years, the proportion of people of colour in prison has exploded. And when they get out, social reintegration is a major challenge for them. Former inmates agreed to share their experiences with La Converse.
Québécois d’origine algérienne, Amine* r: A Quebecer of Algerian origin, Amine* recounts his history with the justice system, visibly shaken. For him, prison is far from an unfamiliar place. “The first time I was arrested was in 2015. I was 15. I was a minor. I got into a fight downtown, and when the police stepped in, they threw me in the backseat of the police car,” says the 23-year-old. “Once we got to the police station, they called my parents to come get me. Nothing happened after that, but I’ll never forget how the cops talked to me in the car. They insulted me and put me down,” he confides, recalling the scene.
Cette première arrestation n’est que le: That first arrest was only the beginning of a stormy relationship between the young man and the justice system. Amine has in fact ended up behind bars at the Montréal Detention Centre, commonly known as “Bordeaux prison,” nine times. “The first time I was in prison was for impaired driving. They arrested me, then took me to the operations centre in downtown Montréal. That’s where I saw a cell for the first time as an adult. I had just turned 18,” he says. The operations centre is where potential suspects are held temporarily. “The cell was empty: there was just a bench and a sink. Since it was winter, it was very cold,” the young man continues. “Normally, if the detention is long, the officers have to give you food, and a blanket if it’s cold, but I got nothing,” he says, indignant. He would get no blanket and would receive food only at the end of the day. “From that moment on, I knew I wasn’t going to be treated like a human being,” he laments.
« Lors de l’un de mes passages à Bordeau: “During one of my stays at Bordeaux, I was put in total isolation in my cell for two weeks. I wasn’t allowed to shower or talk on the phone, because I was locked up alone,” he recalls, worn down by the memory. He also talks about the time when the pandemic was ravaging the world. According to him, people “tend to forget that prison life during that time was especially gruelling.” In a tense tone, he explains: “When someone is sick, they lock down the whole wing. That means you can’t go out for 14 days. If you get sick, the people in your wing forbid you from telling the guards. Otherwise, you turn everyone against you.” Although the general population was struggling with pandemic health restrictions at the time, Amine, who was going in and out of prison during that period, felt great relief each time he returned to the outside world. “When I got out of prison during the pandemic, it was different. Outside, people didn’t live through the pandemic like those in prison did,” he points out.
Tout comme le processus d’incarcération,: Like the process of incarceration, the process of release is disorienting. “I was locked up in an unfamiliar place, with people I didn’t know, and I had no right to anything from the outside world,” he says, describing the social isolation he experienced. He adds that “prisoners are abandoned, and then released; they’re expected to act like rehabilitated citizens. The problem with social reintegration is that no tools are provided for the transition after a short incarceration.” Amine stresses that the length of imprisonment is not the only factor to consider in an inmate’s experience. “Even though I was inside for only a few days, I went through traumatic experiences,” he says, troubled.
Il témoigne de la rupture brutale qu’il: He describes the abrupt break from society that he experienced because of his time in prison. Once released, he was left to fend for himself, with no help to reintegrate into society. “When I got out of prison, someone was supposed to pick me up. I had to go straight home, as if nothing had happened, without being welcomed or guided,” the young man says. For him, the lack of a proper transition only made his situation worse. “Several times, I fell back into the same habits of exclusion.”
Après avoir été confronté aux systèmes j: After being confronted with the justice and prison systems, Amine lost all trust in the institutions connected to them. “I don’t believe in reintegration anymore, it never worked for me,” he admits. With a nonchalant look, he adds: “The way I was treated by the police and the officers made me understand that reintegration isn’t applied the same way for everyone.” This indifference has become a reality shared by other inmates with similar stories. “It’s the result of systemic abandonment. If society doesn’t want me, I won’t try to reintegrate,” he says, resigned.
Comme Amine, Mattéo a été en prison à pl: Like Amine, Mattéo has been in prison several times in his life. Of Mexican origin, the young man is completing a civil engineering technology diploma at Collège Ahuntsic in the hope of taking his life back into his own hands.
Le Québécois de 28 ans connaît bien les: The 28-year-old Quebecer knows the ups and downs of life in the justice system well, having spent many stints in prison all over Quebec. “The first time I was incarcerated, it lasted a month. I had to miss classes and exams,” he explains. His time in detention still gets in the way of his studies. “I had to be absent because of my sentence, which hurt my grades. When I tried to cancel my semester, the school refused. They justified the refusal by telling me that if I had been in prison, it was my own fault. Today, I’ve been found not guilty in that case,” he laments. “I’ve always loved school. I never quit CEGEP, even though it would have been easier for me to drop out,” Mattéo adds with determination.
Les conséquences de son incarcération ne: The consequences of his incarceration aren’t limited to school. He still faces difficulties when looking for a job. In his view, the biggest obstacle to social reintegration is the criminal record attached to a person. “I’ve applied for hundreds of jobs. But every time, I ended up facing a wall,” he admits. “My criminal record is always throwing a wrench in the works. The only jobs I can get are too restrictive and only pay a meagre wage. Otherwise, I can work under the table, but that’s too dangerous,” he continues.
Toujours à la recherche d’un emploi, Mat: Still looking for work, Mattéo faces rejection after rejection. “I was once laughed at in an interview because I had said I had a criminal record,” he says. Filled with frustration, he wonders: “How are you supposed to get back into the job market when you’re a former inmate and you have a label permanently stuck on your back?” Despite his efforts, the former prisoner says he will probably never get the chance to work as an engineer in Quebec. “If I want to get into the Ordre des ingénieurs du Québec, I’ll have to apply for a pardon to have my criminal record suspended. But that won’t be possible for 10 years,” says the student, despairing at the absurdity of the situation.
<strong>« La prison, peu importe la duré: “Prison, no matter how long, leaves deep scars”
Contrairement à Amine et à Mattéo, Elias: Unlike Amine and Mattéo, Elias* has been in prison only once, in 2021. Only 22 years old at the time, he was arrested and taken to the Ottawa-Carleton Detention Centre. He was incarcerated for 25 days. That may sound brief, but for the young man, the experience means long hours locked in a cramped cell, bland food, loneliness and uncertainty.
Une fois libéré, Elias s’est senti délai: Once released, Elias felt abandoned and experienced a great deal of anxiety during his reintegration. “They tell me I’m acquitted of the charges against me. I go back to my cell, I wait for the administrative process to be completed. Then the guards come and finally escort me to freedom,” he describes. He recalls his last moments in prison: “As I walked toward the exit, I could feel the officers’ eyes on me. As if I didn’t deserve that freedom,” he says bitterly. “After 25 nights in the same place, I found myself outside, finally! My parents came to pick me up as if they were picking me up from school, and I went home,” he says, shaken by the lack of sensitivity in the release procedure. He goes on to denounce the fact that there was “no support, no help, no accommodation – not for me, not for my parents.”
Tout au long du trajet de retour chez lu: All the way home, Elias kept wondering about his fate. Having spent time in prison, he wondered anxiously what the repercussions of his experience would be. “The road to Montréal was long. I was happy, but at the same time super anxious; I didn’t know what was going to happen,” he adds, worn down. Fear of the unknown was eating away at the young Montrealer.
« La plus grande épreuve que j’aie endur: “The hardest thing I’ve had to endure is the brutal shock of the transition. Going into prison was painful, but getting out was just as hard,” admits Elias. Feeling abandoned by the system, he continues: “I had no idea what would come next, I was in a fog of stress.” After trying to reintegrate into society, he found himself stuck. “I had conditions to respect. A curfew, for example, which prevented me from having a job. No one wanted to hire me because I couldn’t work after 8 p.m.,” he says. In his view, the treatment inflicted on former inmates is unjust. “I can’t understand how people are released from prison without the slightest help to reintegrate into society after such a traumatic experience. Prison, no matter the length of the sentence, leaves deep scars,” he concludes with conviction.
Les histoires d’Amine, de Mattéo et d’El: The stories of Amine, Mattéo and Elias reflect the frustrating and alarming reality experienced by many people who have served prison sentences. These individuals often struggle to be seen as full human beings. In general, they are instead judged as lifelong delinquents and condemned to live with heavy social stigma.
Mohamed Lotfi, qui est intervenant, éduc: Mohamed Lotfi, a community worker, educator and facilitator who works with former inmates, has heard similar stories and experiences from racialized people. Drawing on his experience, he has observed that “the difficulties former inmates face are often the same as before their incarceration.” In his view, these are in fact the repercussions of various mechanisms that certain communities come up against.
Il souligne également un fait important: He also points out an important fact: “Racial profiling, discrimination, social exclusion – all of that is another form of prison. Prison is just the physical and legal place some individuals end up in, but there are many kinds of systems of exclusion that these same individuals experience every day.” Highlighting the role of this exclusion, Mr. Lotfi continues: “If some people experience social rejection from the very start of their lives, it’s only natural that they’re more at risk of ending up incarcerated. So if a person is five times more likely to be stopped by the police because of the colour of their skin, we’re bound to see an overrepresentation of inmates of colour in prison.” Along the same lines, he adds “that once they’re caught in the cycle of exclusion, the people affected find it harder and harder to get out and return to society with dignity.”
Selon l’éducateur, l’un des principaux o: According to the educator, one of the main obstacles to social reintegration is the exclusion of incarcerated people from public debate. “Prisons and the people who pass through them are completely forgotten. In the media and political spheres, they’re never talked about, or very rarely,” he specifies.
Les difficultés rencontrées par les anci: The difficulties faced by former inmates aren’t limited to their time in prison, but often extend well beyond it. The prison system is organized around a set of mechanisms that have considerable repercussions on people’s lives, particularly those from marginalized or racialized communities. As a solution, the community worker proposes “including the people concerned in decisions and debates in order to find out what they need to reintegrate into society.” In the meantime, Amine, Mattéo and Elias stand in for the many people who, in the same situations, are still waiting for progress.
